tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Read (pp. 55–57): read-aloud of the informational text with new words.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the topic by asking students if they have ever seen Braille script on elevator buttons or currency notes. Accept a few responses to build curiosity about how blind people read.

Read the informational text 'Braille' aloud from the textbook (pp. 55–57) at an unhurried pace, pausing at key moments — Louis's accident, his arrival at the institute, and the invention itself. Draw attention to the new words blacksmith, blind, pincushions, and invented as they appear in the text.

Direct students to look at the full Braille alphabet diagram on p. 56 while you point out two or three letter patterns. Invite students to notice how each letter is made of raised dots arranged in different positions.
Close by asking students to name one fact they found most surprising in the text. Accept two or three brief spoken responses to check first-encounter understanding.

periods.teacher_notes: Take the read-aloud slowly around Louis's accident — the detail that the injury spread from one eye to both is important for understanding why he became totally blind. The new word 'pincushions' benefits from a quick mime or physical gesture showing a cushion with pins pressed into it. Students at this stage absorb the arc of a life story better when they can picture each scene, so pause and invite a quick mental image before moving on.
materials: Blackboard or chart with new words: blacksmith, blind, pincushions, invented

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think A (p. 58): answer three comprehension questions about Braille and Night Writing.

time_bands.activity: Begin with a brief re-recite of the text's key events: Louis's accident, his schooling in Paris, his encounter with Night Writing, and his invention. Students contribute one sentence each as you build a spoken summary on the board.

Pose the first two comprehension questions — describing the Braille alphabet and explaining why Night Writing was not a success — as a shared class discussion. Write key phrases students offer on the board to model answer construction.

Take up the third question — what Louis Braille did to make reading easier for the blind — through guided discussion. Help students frame a complete answer using the board notes, then have them write their own response in their notebooks.

Read out two or three student responses aloud and invite brief peer feedback on whether the answer is complete. Highlight the closing line of the text — 'Thus, a blind person taught the world to see' — and ask what students think it means.

periods.teacher_notes: The question about Night Writing often draws vague answers such as 'it was hard.' Guide students toward the specific reason from the text: it was too complex to be widely adopted, because it used raised dots and dashes that did not map simply to the alphabet. The closing line of the text is worth dwelling on — it rewards a moment of genuine reflection rather than a factual answer.

periods.activity_title: Think and Discuss: Blindness in Everyday Life

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think B (p. 58): discuss why white canes are used and imagined darkness difficulties.

time_bands.activity: Invite students to think quietly for a moment about whether they have ever seen someone using a white cane. Ask one or two students to share what they noticed before opening the formal discussion.

Pose the first discussion question: why is the cane used by people with blindness always white-coloured? Invite students to hypothesise freely, then guide them toward reasons of visibility and international recognition as a symbol. Encourage complete sentences in responses.

Move to the second discussion question: imagine the world goes dark for a day — what difficulties might people face? Conduct a structured pair-share first, then open to the whole class. List difficulties on the board as they emerge — movement, cooking, reading, safety — to show how vision underpins daily life.
Draw the discussion together by asking students to name one thing from the discussion that made them think differently about life without sight. Take two or three responses to close the conversation.

periods.teacher_notes: The white cane question has no single textbook answer — accept any reasoned response that links colour to visibility or to serving as a recognised signal for others. The second question often unlocks rich personal connections; students who mention nighttime difficulties are a useful bridge because 'no light at all, always' is harder to imagine than a familiar dark. Keep the class focused on completing sentences rather than calling out single words.

periods.activity_title: Touch and Tell: Describing Objects Without Sight

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak (pp. 58–59): close eyes, feel an object, complete and share description sentences.

time_bands.activity: Ask students to look around the classroom and name two or three objects within reach. Then explain that today they will describe an object using only touch — no looking allowed once it is in their hand.

Instruct students to close their eyes, pick up one small object from their desk or pencil box, and feel it carefully for about a minute. They then complete the three given sentence frames in their notebooks: shape, length compared to their forefinger, and the object's name.

Students add two more sentences of their own describing the object — texture, weight, or any other quality they noticed by touch. Pair them up to share their descriptions aloud; the listener tries to picture the object from the description alone.

Invite four or five students to share their full descriptions with the class. After each description, ask whether it gave listeners enough information to picture the object, and prompt the speaker to add detail if needed.

periods.teacher_notes: This activity builds directly on the chapter's central insight that the sense of touch can carry information the eyes normally handle — the same insight that drove Louis Braille's invention. Students sometimes rush the sentence frames; encourage them to slow down and notice one more thing about the object before writing. Praise descriptions that use specific shape or texture words rather than 'round' or 'hard' alone.
materials: Small classroom objects (eraser, pencil, sharpener, coin — one per student)

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen (p. 59): listen and repeat words with consonant cluster 'spl' and 'sp'.

time_bands.activity: Write 'sp' and 'spl' on the board and ask students to say each cluster slowly with you three times. Explain that today's listening focuses on words that begin with these clusters, and that careful listening comes before repeating.

Read aloud each word from the textbook word list (p. 59) — spoon, splinter, spin, splash, speak, split, space, splendid — slowly and clearly, stressing the consonant cluster at the start. Repeat the full list three to four times, pausing after each word for students to listen without repeating on the first pass.

Read the list a second time, word by word, and have students repeat each word in unison after you. Then do a choral repetition of the full list twice at a natural pace, ensuring the cluster sounds distinct and not blended into the vowel.

Call on individual students to repeat one word each from the list. After each repetition, confirm the cluster sound or gently model the correction. Close with a quick show of hands: which words begin with 'spl' and which with 'sp' only?

periods.teacher_notes: The cluster 'spl' is the focal phonics point; 'sp' words in the list (spoon, spin, speak, space) are included so students learn to distinguish the two clusters by ear, not just by sight. Read each word at a natural speed — exaggerating the cluster too much can distort the sound model. Students who conflate 'spl' with 'sl' or 'pl' need a second slow model rather than a correction.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write A (p. 60): write Cat, Man, Boy, Jug and own name using Braille dot patterns.

time_bands.activity: Return to the Braille alphabet diagram on p. 56 and walk the class through two or three letter patterns together, showing how the dot positions change for each letter. Point out the example already completed in the textbook on p. 60 before students attempt their own.

Students work through the four given words — Cat, Man, Boy, Jug — using the Braille alphabet chart to look up each letter and reproduce its dot pattern using bindis or pencil dots in the space provided. Move around the room and check that students are reading the chart correctly for each letter.

Students write their own names in Braille dot patterns, looking up each letter of their name individually. Encourage them to check each pattern against the chart before pressing the bindi or drawing the dots.
Pair students to check one word each in their partner's work against the chart. Ask one or two students to share which letter pattern they found most interesting or tricky.

periods.teacher_notes: This writing task is a direct encounter with the chapter's subject matter — students experience the one-symbol-per-letter logic Louis Braille invented. Watch for students who try to work from memory rather than referring to the chart for each letter; redirect them back to p. 56. Names with unusual letter combinations (Q, X, Z) will naturally take longer — this is a good moment to appreciate the Braille alphabet's completeness.
materials: Bindis or pencils for dot patterns

periods.activity_title: Writing to Protect: Eye Safety Precautions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write B (p. 61): list precautions to protect eyes from harm, linked to Louis Braille's story.

time_bands.activity: Recall for the class how Louis Braille lost his sight — a sharp tool in his father's blacksmith workshop pierced his eye when he was three years old. Ask students to think of sharp or dangerous things they or family members handle at home or during festivals that could harm eyes.

Model the writing task aloud: think out loud about one precaution (e.g. 'wear protective goggles when near sharp tools') and write it on the board as a complete sentence beginning with a capital letter. Show students how a list is structured — each point is a separate, clearly worded sentence.

Students independently draft their own list of precautions to protect eyes from harm, writing at least four complete sentences. Circulate and prompt students who are stuck by asking: what could cause an eye injury at home, during play, during festivals?

Invite three or four students to read one precaution each from their lists. After each, ask the class if it is clear and complete. Encourage any revision students feel is needed and have them make it before closing their notebooks.

periods.teacher_notes: The textbook's reference to a child losing an eye while lighting firecrackers gives this task immediate real-world weight — use that connection to motivate genuine thinking rather than generic list-making. Students who produce very short sentences ('Don't touch eyes') should be guided to expand: what should one do instead, or in what situation. Model the expansion on the board with one such sentence before releasing students to write independently.

periods.activity_title: Past Continuous Tense: Was/Were + Action Word

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn C (pp. 61–62): change present continuous sentences to past continuous using was/were.

time_bands.activity: Write the example sentence from the textbook on the board: 'Long ago, in France, a little boy named Louis Braille was playing near his home.' Ask students what tense this is and how they know. Establish that 'was + action word + ing' shows something happening in the past over a period of time, and introduce the singular/plural distinction: 'was' for one, 'were' for more than one.

Work through the model example from p. 61 together ('I am sleeping → I was sleeping'), then take up the next two sentences from the exercise as a shared task, with students contributing the change orally before you write it on the board. Highlight the pattern each time: remove 'am/are', add 'was/were'.

Students complete the remaining four sentences from the exercise independently in their notebooks. Circulate and check that students are applying the singular/plural rule correctly — 'we are playing' → 'we were playing' is a common stumbling point.

Review the last two answers together as a class. Ask a student who used 'were' correctly to explain to the class why they chose 'were' rather than 'was'. Affirm the reasoning and correct any remaining errors.

periods.teacher_notes: The textbook roots this grammar point in the chapter's own first sentence about Louis Braille — use that anchor to show students that grammar emerges from real texts, not from nowhere. The most common error is using 'was' for plural subjects ('We was playing'); make the plural examples visible on the board throughout. Students who finish early can write two original sentences of their own in the past continuous.

periods.activity_title: Picture Story: Past Continuous in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn D (pp. 62–63): fill blanks in Tarandeep's picture story using past continuous forms.

time_bands.activity: Draw students' attention to the five-panel picture story on pp. 62–63 and walk through the images panel by panel: a girl with squirrels and sparrows, grains being scattered, a grandmother hanging clothes, wind blowing, and animals sitting on clothes. Ask students to narrate what they see in each panel before reading any text.

Read the full story text aloud from the textbook, leaving each blank unsaid. After each blank, ask students to look at the picture for that moment and predict which option from the word box fits. Write student predictions on the board without confirming right or wrong yet.

Students complete the six blanks in their notebooks using the given word box: was feeding, was scattering, was hanging, was entering, were sitting, was clapping. They check each choice against the picture and the singular/plural rule before writing.

Go through the answers together, asking a different student to read each completed sentence aloud and explain why they chose 'was' or 'were' for that blank. Affirm correct reasoning and address any remaining confusion about the singular/plural distinction.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked with was/were + action word in the grammar exercise, students now apply that same structure in the richer context of a picture story — the pictures carry the meaning that confirms or corrects each choice. 'Were sitting' is the key item where students must apply the plural rule; if several students default to 'was sitting', return to the picture and count the animals together. The story about Tarandeep, squirrels, and sparrows is light and enjoyable — let students enjoy it rather than treating it purely as a grammar drill.

periods.activity_title: Feel the Shape: Making Raised Impressions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do (p. 64): press shapes on paper, feel raised surface with eyes closed, guess with a friend.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the activity by linking it to the Braille system: just as Louis Braille's dot patterns are felt by touch, today students will create raised impressions on paper and feel them with their fingertips. Demonstrate pressing a circle on paper using the back of a pencil, then running a finger over the raised side.

Each student takes a sheet of paper and presses one shape or letter firmly using a matchstick end or pencil back — a circle, a plus sign, or any letter. They then close their eyes, flip the paper over, and run a finger over the raised surface to try to identify what they drew.

Students swap their papers with a partner without revealing the shape. The partner closes their eyes and tries to identify the raised impression by touch alone, then shares what they think it is. They reveal and discuss whether the guess was correct.

Gather the class and ask three or four pairs to share whether the shape was guessed correctly and what made it easy or hard to identify by touch. Connect this back to why the Braille system uses a small, consistent six-dot cell — too many variations make recognition by touch much harder.

periods.teacher_notes: This activity gives students a direct, embodied experience of what reading by touch demands — connecting the chapter's intellectual content to a physical sensation. Simple shapes work better than complex letters for a first attempt; students who choose letters with curved strokes (S, G, C) often find them harder to identify by feel and this is itself a useful discovery. If white clay is available, it can substitute for paper and offers a more striking tactile result.

periods.activity_title: Being an Ally: Supporting Classmates with Low Vision

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Explore (p. 64): discuss ways to assist classmates with low vision as a thoughtful friend.

homework.task_brief: Let us Explore (p. 64): find out the name and location of the nearest resource centre for people with blindness.

time_bands.activity: Open by asking students to think about what it might be like to sit in class and not be able to see the board clearly, or to need to hold a book very close to their face to read it. Give students a quiet moment to think before sharing.

Discuss what low vision means and how students with low vision might experience everyday classroom activities differently from students with full sight. Accept a range of responses and build a short list on the board: reading, board work, group tasks, moving around the room.

Students work in small groups to brainstorm at least three practical ways they could assist a classmate with low vision — for example, offering to read a board note aloud, sharing a large-print version of a worksheet, or sitting close to help them follow a lesson. Groups share their ideas with the class.

Close with a brief whole-class reflection: which idea surprised you most, or which one do you think you could actually start doing? Set the homework — find the name and location of the nearest resource centre for people with blindness — and explain that students may ask family members or search with an adult's help.

periods.teacher_notes: This discussion moves from the chapter's historical story of Louis Braille to the students' own classroom reality — the chapter's invitation to see the world through another person's experience. Students sometimes conflate low vision with complete blindness; clarify that low vision means reduced but not absent sight, which is why large fonts, clear seating, and brighter lighting can genuinely help. The homework is an exploratory, family-supported task rather than a written assignment.

periods.activity_title: Chapter Synthesis: From One Boy's Invention to Our World

time_bands.activity: Open by inviting students to retell the story of Louis Braille in their own words — his accident, his schooling in Paris, his encounter with Night Writing, and his creation of the Braille alphabet. Accept contributions from several students to build a collective spoken summary.

Revisit the past continuous tense in a quick whole-class activity: call out present continuous sentences connected to Louis Braille's life — 'Louis is playing near the workshop' — and have students change each to the past continuous aloud. Take four or five examples to consolidate the was/were pattern.

Students write three to four sentences describing what Louis Braille was doing at a key moment in the story — for example, when he was at the Royal Institute, or when he was simplifying the Night Writing system — using the past continuous correctly. They write independently and complete within the time available.

Pose a closing discussion question connecting to the chapter's broader themes: if you could tell Louis Braille one thing about how his invention is used in the world today, what would you say? Invite three or four students to respond in complete sentences.

Close with a tactile challenge: write two or three letters on the board in Braille dot notation and ask students to decode them using their knowledge of the Braille alphabet. Celebrate the chapter's central idea together — 'a blind person taught the world to see' — and invite students to say what that line means to them now.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis draws together the chapter's informational content, grammar work, writing practice, and tactile explorations into a single coherent arc. The past continuous retelling activity connects Louis Braille's life story to the grammar the class has practised, showing students that the tense and the text belong together. The closing Braille decoding challenge is celebratory rather than evaluative — it honours what the chapter built and invites students to finish on a note of genuine achievement.

items.source_context: Louis Braille's life, blindness accident, Night Writing encounter, invention of the Braille alphabet.
items.item_stem: Read the statements below. Write True or False for each one, and give one reason for your answer from the passage.

options.text: Captain Charles Barbier's Night Writing used raised dots and dashes.
Louis Braille lost his sight because he was born blind.
Only people who are blind are allowed to read Braille.
The Braille alphabet has one raised-dot symbol for each of the twenty-six letters.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. False — Louis became blind after a sharp tool pierced his eye in his father's workshop and the injury spread to both eyes. 2. True — Night Writing used raised dots and dashes so soldiers could read in the dark. 3. True — Louis simplified the system to one raised-dot symbol per letter of the English alphabet. 4. False — Braille is open to anyone, not only people with blindness.

expected_elements: Reference to Louis Braille creating the Braille alphabet.
Idea that his invention helped many people beyond the blind.
Personal interpretation of 'teaching the world to see'.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. True — splash begins with spl. 2. False — speak begins with sp only. 3. True — split begins with spl. 4. False — spoon begins with sp only. 5. True — splendid begins with spl. 6. False — spin begins with sp only.

items.item_stem: Choose the correct past continuous form to complete each sentence.

options.label: A
options.text: All three sentences above use the past continuous form correctly.

options.label: B
options.text: Louis Braille was study / was studying / were studying in Paris when he learnt about Night Writing. — The correct form is: was studying

options.label: C
options.text: She was writing / were writing / is writing a letter to her friend last evening. — The correct form is: was writing

options.label: D
options.text: The students were sitting / was sitting / are sitting on the floor during the lesson. — The correct form is: were sitting

what_each_option_reveals.B: Students choosing this may not recognise that 'was studying' is already the correct answer and may be confused by the presentation format.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Students choosing this may not have recognised that 'were sitting' correctly applies to a plural subject.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Students choosing this may be uncertain about the singular subject rule and may default to any 'was' form without checking.

items.item_stem: Louis Braille's invention showed that a person with blindness could find a way to help the whole world. Think of one thing you could do — at school, at home, or in your neighbourhood — to make life a little easier for someone who cannot see well. Tell the class what you would do and why you think it would help.

expected_elements: Names one specific, practical action to help.
Explains clearly why the action would help.
Speaks in complete sentences with a clear idea.
